Defamation or Legitimate Criticism? What Can Be Removed Online in Italy

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

In Italy, a harsh review or a sharp opinion is usually lawful criticism, while a false statement of fact that damages someone's reputation can be defamation. The distinction rests on three tests developed by Italian courts: truth of the facts, measured language (continenza) and relevance to a matter of interest. Only content that fails them, or that breaks a platform's own rules, can realistically be removed.

Facts versus opinions: where the line runs

The key question is whether a statement can be proven true or false. “The service was slow and the food mediocre” is an opinion based on personal experience; “the restaurant uses frozen fish and sells it as fresh” is a factual claim that is either true or not. Opinions enjoy wide protection, false facts do not.

Defamation under art. 595 of the Italian Criminal Code occurs when someone offends another person's reputation while communicating with several people, and the penalty is increased when the offence is committed through the press or any other means of publicity, which courts apply to websites, social networks and review platforms. Against this stands the right of criticism (diritto di critica), rooted in art. 21 of the Constitution and treated as the lawful exercise of a right under art. 51 c.p. Every case of defamation on the internet is a balance between these two principles.

The three conditions for lawful criticism

Italian case law has long held that criticism is lawful when it meets three conditions together. If any of them fails, the protection weakens or disappears, and content that is otherwise a legitimate opinion may become defamatory.

Truth (verità)

The facts on which the criticism is based must be true, or at least reasonably believed to be true after proper checking. A customer who writes that a hotel charged more than the agreed price must be describing something that actually happened. The opinion that follows, for example that the hotel is dishonest in its pricing, does not need to be “true”, but it cannot rest on invented facts.

Measured language (continenza)

The form must be proportionate. Strong, even sarcastic words are allowed, especially when criticising a business or a public figure, but gratuitous insults, personal attacks unrelated to the subject and degrading expressions go beyond criticism. Calling a meal “a disaster” is continent; calling the owner a criminal without any basis is not.

Relevance (pertinenza)

The criticism must concern something of legitimate interest to readers, such as the quality of a service, the conduct of a professional or the decisions of a company. Comments on the private life, family or health of a business owner, unrelated to the service, rarely pass this test.

Clear examples: what stays and what can go

Applied to real content, the three tests produce fairly predictable results. The examples below reflect how Italian platforms and courts typically treat common situations, though each case depends on its exact wording and context.

StatementClassificationLikely outcome
“Waited 40 minutes, pasta overcooked, not coming back.”Opinion on own experienceStays
“Worst dentist in Rome, avoid at all costs.”Harsh but continent criticismUsually stays
“They charged me more than the price list said.” (documented)True factStays
“This clinic operates without a licence.” (false)False statement of factDefamatory, removable
“The owner is a thief and a crook.” (no basis)Insulting accusationDefamatory, removable
Review by someone who was never a customerFake contentRemovable under platform policy

The last row matters in practice. Many requests to remove defamatory reviews succeed not because a platform decides the content is defamatory, but because it clearly breaks the platform's rules on fake engagement, conflicts of interest or off-topic content. The policy route is usually faster than the legal one, as our guide to removing fake reviews on Google Maps explains.

What platforms will remove

Platforms remove content that clearly violates their policies or that is manifestly illegal; they rarely decide disputed questions of fact. Google, Trustpilot, Facebook or TripAdvisor are not courts, and a reviewer's word against a business owner's word will normally leave the content online.

Content that platforms typically take down includes:

  • fake reviews, reviews from competitors or former employees with a conflict of interest, and coordinated review attacks;
  • hate speech, threats, obscene language and harassment;
  • personal data such as phone numbers, addresses or health information about identifiable people;
  • content found unlawful by a court or an authority, once the decision is submitted.

Under the Digital Services Act, hosting services must provide a notice-and-action mechanism and handle well-substantiated notices diligently, explaining their decisions. A precise notice, quoting the exact words, explaining why they are false and attaching evidence, has far better chances than a generic complaint. The changes introduced by the DSA are covered in our article on platform liability for third-party content.

What Italian courts will remove

Courts can order removal when content is defamatory, and they are the only realistic route to remove libel online when the platform refuses and the statement is a disputed factual claim. The criminal and civil routes have different aims and timing.

On the criminal side, a complaint (querela) for defamation must generally be filed within three months of learning of the content, with the Carabinieri, the police or the Polizia Postale. During the proceedings, the judge may order the preventive seizure of the web page, which in practice means it is blocked or removed, and investigators can ask platforms to identify anonymous authors. On the civil side, an urgent application under art. 700 c.p.c. can obtain a removal order when there is a risk of serious and irreparable harm, while an ordinary action seeks compensation under art. 2043 c.c. Note that direct insults addressed to a person (ingiuria) are no longer a crime in Italy and lead only to civil consequences.

Courts protect reputation against false facts and gratuitous insults, not against unfavourable opinions. Before taking action, check which of the two you are facing.

Online defamation management: choosing the right response

Good online defamation management starts with classification, not with a legal letter. Treating criticism as defamation often backfires: the threat is published, the story spreads, and the original review gains visibility.

A practical order of steps:

  1. classify each item using the three tests;
  2. preserve evidence with screenshots and, for serious cases, a certified copy of the page;
  3. report clear policy violations to the platform;
  4. reserve legal action for false factual claims that cause real harm.

Legitimate criticism deserves a calm public reply that corrects facts where needed and shows how the issue was handled, following the principles in our guide on responding to negative reviews.
